transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, thank you, doctor. It's... well, I suppose my family is the one who finally pushed me to make the appointment, to be honest with you. I've got a lot of time on my hands these days, not working anymore and all, so I finally agreed to come down here and see what's what. 

What brings me in is this... this reaction I keep having. It's the strangest thing, but whenever I step into an elevator—especially one of those really slow ones, you know the kind in the older buildings that just seem to take forever and make those awful groaning noises?—or if I have to go into a small room where the door gets locked, it just hits me. My chest jumps right away. I mean, the very second I'm in there. It’s like a physical jolt right in the center of my ribs. 

And before I can even think straight, before I can even tell myself that everything is perfectly fine and I'm safe, I get this incredibly strong need to get back out. I just have to turn around and pull on the handle. I don't even have time to reason with myself, it's just this instant, overpowering urge to escape the second that door closes or that elevator starts moving. It's just very unsettling, you know, not being able to control that initial jump in my chest, and it just happens so fast I can't even process it before I'm already trying to leave.
Has this chest jolt and urge to escape ever happened to you in other situations, like in open spaces, crowds, or when you're not in an elevator or small room?

Well, no... no, it really hasn't. It's funny you mention open spaces and crowds, because my sister, Margaret—she's a few years younger than me, lives over in Ohio now—she can't stand a crowd. She won't go to a parade, won't go to a busy grocery store on a Sunday. But me? I don't mind that at all. I can be right in the middle of a bustling market, shoulder to shoulder with folks, and I feel perfectly fine. I actually sort of like the energy of it, to be honest. 

And open spaces, well, I used to love just sitting out in the wide open fields when we lived out in the country back when I was a boy. Never bothered me a bit. It's strictly... it's strictly the small, closed-in places. Like I said, those elevators. Or even—and I didn't mention this before, but it's true—sometimes even a small bathroom if there's no window and the fan isn't running. If it just feels too still and too tight, and I know that door is shut tight behind me... that's when it happens. But out in the open? Or in a big hall with lots of people? No, I don't get that jump in my chest at all. I feel completely normal, completely like myself. It's just those tight, closed-off spots that set it off. I don't know why, but it's like my body just knows the walls are too close, you know?

When you're in those tight or closed-in places and you feel that chest jolt and the urge to escape, does your heart start racing, do you feel like you can't breathe, or does it feel like something terrible is about to happen?

Well, you know, it's not so much that I feel like I'm having a heart attack or that I can't catch a breath... it's more about what my mind does. It's like... well, let me explain it this way. I remember going to the natural history museum with my grandson a few years back. Beautiful place, really. They had this whole exhibit on the Ice Age, and to get down to the lower level where they kept the big mammoth skeletons, you had to take this little elevator. And they also had these tiny little storage rooms off to the side, where they kept the extra folding chairs and things, and one of the doors was propped open. 

Now, I look at that storage room, or I look at that elevator, and the logical part of my brain—the part that's lived almost eighty years on this earth—knows perfectly well that it's just a room. It's just a box with cables. I know a little storage room or an elevator at the museum isn't the same as being locked up in a dungeon or something awful like that. But my mind... my mind just treats it like absolute trouble the very minute I see there's no window and I know that door is going to shut tight. 

It's just this overwhelming sense of... of wrongness. Like an alarm bell going off in my head saying, "You shouldn't be in here, this isn't right, you need to leave right now." It doesn't matter if it's a perfectly safe museum elevator or a little bathroom at a diner. The second that door closes and I realize I'm closed in, my mind just decides it's a terrible situation. I don't necessarily feel like I'm dying or anything dramatic like that, but I just feel this incredible, immediate push that I have to get out of that box before something bad *does* happen, even though I know, deep down, it's just a room. It's very frustrating, having your brain tell you one thing when your common sense tells you another.
When you feel that chest jolt and the urge to escape, do you notice your heart racing, feel like you can't catch your breath, or worry that something really bad like a heart attack might happen?

Well, like I was trying to say just a moment ago, it's really not like that. I don't... I don't feel like I'm having a heart attack, no. I know some folks get that way. My buddy Earl, he had a heart attack back in '98, said it felt like an elephant was sitting on his chest, couldn't breathe, the whole nine yards. But for me in those elevators, it's not like that. 

I don't really notice my heart racing like a runaway train or anything, and I can breathe just fine, physically speaking. I'm not gasping for air or clutching my chest thinking my time is up. It's just that initial jolt I mentioned, right in the ribs, and then it's all up here in my head. It's the mind playing tricks, telling me I've got to get out, get out, get out. It's not a worry about my body failing me, it's a worry about the space itself. I just don't have those physical things you're asking about, the racing heart or the shortness of breath. It's just that intense, immediate need to pull the handle and walk back out into the hallway.
When you're not in an elevator or a small room, do you find yourself worrying or thinking a lot about those spaces, or are you only bothered by them when you're actually in the situation?

Well, no, I can't say that I do. I don't sit around stewing over it, that's for sure. Take yesterday, for example. I was sitting out on the back porch, reading the paper—well, reading what's left of the paper these days, they've cut it down to practically nothing, just a few pages of local news and the crossword puzzle. I do try to do the crossword, keeps the mind sharp, you know, especially at my age. But anyway, I was sitting there for a good two hours, enjoying the breeze, and I didn't have a single thought in my head about elevators or tiny rooms or any of that business. 

It just doesn't cross my mind when I'm going about my regular day. I sleep just fine, too. I don't lie awake at night staring at the ceiling, dreading the next time I might have to go into a small space or worrying about getting stuck. I just go about my business, go down to the hardware store, visit with my neighbor Tom—he's got this old Ford tractor he's been fixing up for about five years now, we talk about that a lot. 

It's really only when I'm right there, standing in front of those sliding metal doors, or when I walk into a room and suddenly realize how tight the walls are and that the door's closing behind me. That's the only time it hits me. Out of sight, out of mind, as my father used to say. If I'm not looking right at it or stepping into it, it's like it doesn't even exist in my world. So no, I don't fret about it ahead of time. I've got plenty of other things to occupy my time, what with the garden needing weeding and the grandkids coming over on the weekends.
Have you ever had sudden, intense episodes of fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, where you felt like something terrible was happening to you, even if you couldn't explain why?

Well, no... no, I can't say I've ever had anything like that happen. You mean just out of the clear blue sky? Like you're just sitting there minding your own business and suddenly the world is ending for no good reason? No, no. I'm a pretty steady fellow, all things considered. 

Now, my late wife, God rest her soul, she used to get these spells sometimes where she'd just feel completely overwhelmed out of nowhere, especially right after her sister passed away back in '04. She'd have to sit down at the kitchen table and fan herself with a magazine, said she felt like a dark cloud just dropped right on top of her and she couldn't explain why she was so upset. It was hard to watch, it really was. But me? I've never been wired that way. 

Like I was telling you before about sitting on the porch with the newspaper... my days are just very quiet and even-keeled. I get up, I make my coffee—just half a cup of the regular stuff these days mixed with decaf, doctor's orders on account of my blood pressure creeping up a little bit a couple years back, though honestly I think the machine at the grocery store pharmacy was just broken that day because it's been fine ever since. But anyway, I don't get these sudden scares you're talking about. Unless I'm looking right at a closed-in space where I know I'm going to be trapped, my nerves are steady as a rock. I don't just suddenly get terrified for no reason at all. There's always got to be a reason, and for me, it's just those tight little boxes. If I'm not in one of those, I'm right as rain. Never had a sudden fright like you're describing.
